content_metadata.description: The video details the total synthesis of resveratrol and its derivatives, focusing on the chemical processes, potential applications, and research insights.

qAndA.question: What is the name of the reaction used to create the alkene bond in resveratrone?
What property makes resveratrone a potential candidate for a biological label?
How many equivalents of the boronic ester precursor were initially required for the epoxide olefination?
What chemical group is installed in iso-resveratrone to make it click-ready?

qAndA.answer: The epoxide precursor was more valuable than the boronic ester in this case, justifying the excess.
qAndA.question: Why was a greater excess of boronic ester used for the epoxide olefination in the synthesis of the azide derivative?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: In this video we'll take a look at the first total synthesis of reservoir drone and two
interesting reservoir drone derivatives.
During this work we learned some important lessons about our epoxide olefination reaction
which gave us a better idea about its mechanism and thus allowed us to do some further optimization.
But first things first, what is reservoir drone?
You will probably have heard about reservoir drone.
It and a couple of other hydroxys stillbans have risen to some prominence as ingredients
of red wine to which several healthy benefits were attributed.
And who doesn't like to hear that the daily glass of wine isn't a boozing habit but
the valiant act protecting one's cardiovascular system?
Well, unfortunately we have to pour some water into your wine here.
These health benefits seem somewhat debatable.
But we are not here to talk about reservoir drone, but reservoir drone.
Reservoir drone can be generated from reservoir drone by irradiating it with UV light.
This results in a highly fluorescent molecule and the interesting thing about reservoir
drone is that there is some evidence that it allows for two photon absorption.
Before we start talking about the synthesis, let's have a quick and very basic recap of
fluorescence in order to see why this is so interesting.
Usually it takes absorption of a photon with quite a lot of energy to excite a fluorescent
molecule.
In order to revert to the ground state, some energy is usually emitted as heat, so the photon
that is re-emitted has less energy and thus a higher wavelength than the photon which
was absorbed.
That's why we usually use UV lamps to excite fluorescent molecules.
However, this is far from ideal for biological applications, as many cells don't really like
being smashed with UV light.
Two, photon absorption on the other hand proceeds via a virtual state which is kind of halfway
between the ground state and the excited state.
This means that a photon with less energy is required to reach this virtual state.
But from it, a second low energy photon is enough to reach the excited state from which
fluorescence can occur.
So a longer wavelengths can be used to excite molecules that allow for two photon absorption,
which makes res-retron an interesting candidate for a biological label.
So, how can we get our hands on it?
Res-retron was isolated and named by Kim and co-workers after irradiation of trans-res-retron
and isolation by preparative TLC.
They also proposed a mechanism for this photochemical transformation.
Since the relationship between res-retron and res-retron is not that obvious, we color-coded
the relevant parts.
Their mechanistic proposal relies on its cis-transitomerization, which is followed by a six-pie
electrocyclic ring closure that closes the naphthalene moiety.
In order to break up the blue cyclohexadiene, a second electrocyclic ring closure is proposed,
which builds up this blue bicyclohexanol.
A total memorization to the corresponding ketone generates a classic fragmentation precursor
in which the carbonyl group acts as an electron sink and the binologous enol acts as an electron
donor.
And the product of this fragmentation is only two total memorizations away from res-retron.
So, it is possible to make res-retron from cheaply available res-retron this way.
However, the synthesis is quite cumbersome and involves large solvent volumes and extensive
purification.
Therefore, developing a total synthesis for this molecule seemed quite attractive.
For this, we envisioned a globally protected intermediate which could in turn be made from
enough two boronic acid, derivative and a known epoxide precursor by using our epoxide
olefination reaction.
This olefination, which was published by us in 2019, relies on the lithiation of an epoxide
and sub-sequent formation of an 8 complex with a boronate.
The A complex can then undergo a metasent type 1-2 rearrangement which delivers a beta-alcoxy
boronate which then undergo some type of zoon elimination upon heating.
The cute thing about this chemistry is that the resulting alkene could be turned back into
an epoxide again so that it can be applied iteratively.
However, there is a problem.
In order to get good yields out of this reaction, two equivalents of the boronate precursor are usually
necessary.
The reason for this might very well be that the alkoxide that results from the 1-2 rearrangement
reacts with another equivalent of the boronic acid.
That means if the 1-2 rearrangement which could also be catalyzed by excess boronate is
as fast or even faster than the A complex formation, one molecule of lithiated epoxide will

The second equivalent of boronic acid is re-liberated after the elimination but for alkyl substituted
alkene that requires heating.
And since a lithiated epoxide is a classic carbeneoid, it will certainly not survive such
a harsh treatment.
This was an interesting challenge for our proposed respiratory synthesis as the NAFTA-LINE

But there was some good news as well.
The alkene we were about to make was conjugated to an aromatic system.
And this should speed up the elimination step and thus re-liberate the boronic acid.
We tried this out on a simple styrene derivative first.
For this we were able to reduce the required excess of boronic acid ester to only 1.3
equalids.

by heart-vik miara-boilation.

Which unfortunately is quite typical for this type of substrate.

Nevertheless, with both of these compounds in our hands, we followed Blonsky's procedure
to the required epoxide precursor.
And this one proceeds in very good yields.
We then reacted it with the appropriate NAFTOT boronator derivative and WOLA got the desired
coupling product.
While the yield was less satisfying than with the less electron rich test system, we were
nevertheless able to get our hands on Reseratrone after globally protection of this olefination
product.
Similar yields were also obtained for the regi-isemir, which we called iser-reseratrone here.
However, since the boronic ester necessary for making Reseratrone is somewhat unstable,
it was quite easy to get our hands on the one necessary for making iser-reseratrone.
And since the UV spectra of both compounds looks similar enough, we decided to apply our
synthesis to an iser-reseratrone derivative that can be used for click reactions and thus
might be very useful as a label for biological applications.
Starting from commercially available for bromobuterole chloride, we prepared this propagul

Substitution of the bromide and epoxidation with oxone delivered the necessary epoxide
precursor.
Since here the epoxide was somewhat more precious than the boronic ester, we felt justified
to use a slightly greater axis of boronic ester for the epoxide-oilification.
And this led to a 51% yield based on the epoxide.
This a-zite derivative might serve as an interesting label since it can now be connected to the
alkyne of your choice.
We just used phenyl acetylene as a cheap model substrate here, and we were quite surprised
by the low yield obtained after chromatography.
However, according to mass spec, this was due to partial desilulation of the phenyl ethers
under the aqueous conditions.
So using a different click protocol or avoiding chromatography after this step might be a good
idea.
However, global deep protection under acidic conditions worked very well and furnished
the desired label product.
So if you want to learn more about this chemistry, check out our article available in chemistry
open.
